why_how.text: Colorado ties driving on public roads to two things together: being at least sixteen and carrying a valid license.
New residents and people who change their name or address each get thirty days, so the clock starts with the change.

scenario.text: Maya takes a job in Denver and moves into an apartment there in March.

reasoning.text: Holding a job in Colorado is one example of residency, so the thirty-day licensing clock starts.

result.text: Maya gets her Colorado license within thirty days and reports any later address change within thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a new resident has ninety days to get a Colorado license.

correction.text: Ninety days of continuous living is only a residency example; the licensing deadline is thirty days.

memory_support.text: Sixteen to drive, thirty days to switch.

prompt.text: Maya became a resident when she took her Denver job. How long does she have to get her Colorado license?

answer.text: Thirty days from becoming a resident.

rationale.text: The licensing deadline is thirty days; the ninety-day figure only describes one way to become a resident.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson of the Colorado driver handbook. Before tests, permits or turn signals, the state sets a simple floor for anyone using its public roads. You need to be old enough, and you need a valid license, whether you drive a car, a motor-driven cycle or a moped. Then, if you move here, the state expects you to switch over to a Colorado license on a schedule. This lesson covers who must be licensed, what makes someone a resident, how long a new resident has to get licensed, who is exempt, and how quickly you report a new name or address.

lines.text: Covers cars, motor-driven cycles and mopeds.

narration.text: Here is the rule everything else builds on. Anyone driving a motor vehicle, a motor-driven cycle or a moped on public roads in Colorado has to be at least sixteen years old and carry a valid driver license. Notice that mopeds are not an exception, and notice that both conditions apply together. Being sixteen without a license is not enough, and having a license from somewhere does not help if it is not valid. When a practice question describes a young rider on a small bike, come back to this baseline: age sixteen and a valid license, every time, on any public road.

Colorado gives examples of what makes you a resident rather than a single test. You count as a resident if, for example, you own or run a business in the state, have lived here continuously for ninety days, or hold a job here. Any one of those examples can be enough. Once you are a resident, a deadline starts: you have thirty days to get a Colorado driver license. Some people are not held to that thirty-day deadline, including active-duty military members, their dependents, and people living here mainly to further their education. Keep the examples and the exemptions in separate boxes.

lines.text: Name or address change: thirty days.

narration.text: This is where many learners slip. Three numbers sit close together in this part of the handbook, and two of them are the same. Getting a Colorado license after you become a resident takes thirty days. Reporting a change of name or address to the Division of Motor Vehicles also takes thirty days. The ninety days is different: it is one example of how you become a resident, by living here continuously. So if a question asks how long you have to act, think thirty. If it asks what can make you a resident, ninety days of living here is one answer among several.

Here is a quick check: Maya takes a job in Denver and moves into an apartment there. Holding a job is one of the residency examples, so she is now a Colorado resident. How long does she have to get her Colorado driver license? Work it out before reading on. The answer is thirty days. The ninety-day figure would only matter if residency depended on how long she had lived here, and in her case the job already makes her a resident. If Maya later moves across town, she again has thirty days, this time to tell the Division of Motor Vehicles about the new address.

lines.text: Thirty days to switch or report.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. To drive any motor vehicle, motor-driven cycle or moped on Colorado public roads, you must be at least sixteen and carry a valid license. Owning or running a business, living here continuously for ninety days, or holding a job here are examples of residency. A new resident has thirty days to get a Colorado license, unless they are active-duty military, a military dependent, or here mainly for school. Any change of name or address goes to the Division of Motor Vehicles within thirty days. Next, we look at the written test and the permit it unlocks.

why_how.text: The written test draws on the whole handbook, which is why every chapter matters, not only the signs.
Passing the written test only unlocks an instruction permit, so a supervisor rule follows right away.

scenario.text: Leo wants to take his written test and finds an office that closes at five in the afternoon.

reasoning.text: Offices stop giving written tests thirty minutes before closing, so Leo must start well before half past four.

result.text: Leo arrives early, passes, and gets an instruction permit; his twenty-four-year-old sister supervises from the front passenger seat.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming any licensed sixteen-year-old friend can supervise a permit driver.

correction.text: The driving age is sixteen, but a permit supervisor must be twenty-one or older with a valid Colorado license.

memory_support.text: Pass the test, then permit with a twenty-one-plus coach.

prompt.text: Leo's licensed seventeen-year-old cousin offers to ride along while Leo drives on his permit. Does that work?

answer.text: No. The supervisor must be at least twenty-one, hold a valid Colorado license and sit in the front passenger seat.

rationale.text: Sixteen is the age to drive; twenty-one is the age to supervise a permit driver.

narration.text: In this lesson we move from the basic licensing rules to your first real step: the written knowledge test. You will learn what material the test draws on, a timing rule that catches people at the office door, and what passing actually earns you. Passing does not hand you a full license. It makes you eligible for an instruction permit, and that permit comes with an important condition about who rides with you. By the end you should be able to plan your test visit and explain who may supervise you once you start driving on a permit.

lines.text: The whole handbook is fair game.
Signs, impaired driving, rules, safety, law.

narration.text: The written knowledge test is not limited to one chapter. It draws on the whole handbook, including road signs, driving under the influence, driving rules, safety rules and legal topics. That breadth is a good reason to study every section, not just the sign pages. Colorado also offers practice quizzes online and in the myColorado app, which can help you find weak spots before test day. Think of the handbook as the test outline: if a topic appears in it, a question could be built on it, so your study plan should follow the handbook from start to finish.

Here is a timing trap. Offices stop giving written tests thirty minutes before their scheduled closing time, so you need to arrive earlier than that. Because the last lesson had two thirty-day deadlines, it is easy to blur this rule with them. Keep them apart. The thirty-day rules are deadlines for getting a Colorado license after becoming a resident and for reporting a new name or address. The thirty-minute rule is a scheduling cutoff at the office door. If a question mentions closing time, think minutes and arrive early; if it mentions moving or a name change, think days.

lines.text: Passing makes you eligible for a permit.

narration.text: Once you pass a written test, you become eligible for an instruction permit. The permit gives a learner limited driving privileges, not the freedom of a full license. That word limited matters, because the permit comes with conditions. The most important one is supervision. While you drive on an instruction permit, you need a supervising driver who is twenty-one or older and holds a valid Colorado license, and that person sits in the front passenger seat. A supervisor in the back seat, or one who is too young, does not meet the rule even if they are a careful driver.

Here is a quick check: Leo has just earned his instruction permit. His cousin is seventeen, has a valid license, and offers to ride in the front passenger seat while Leo practices. Does that meet Colorado's rule? Think it through before reading the answer. It does not. A permit supervisor must be at least twenty-one and hold a valid Colorado license, and must sit in the front passenger seat. The cousin is old enough to drive, because the general driving age is sixteen, but not old enough to supervise. Leo's twenty-four-year-old sister, with a valid Colorado license, would work.

Let us review. The written test draws on the whole handbook, and practice quizzes are available online and in the myColorado app. Offices stop giving written tests thirty minutes before closing, so plan to arrive earlier, and do not confuse that cutoff with the thirty-day deadlines. Passing makes you eligible for an instruction permit with limited privileges. On that permit, your supervisor must be twenty-one or older, hold a valid Colorado license, and sit in the front passenger seat. Keep the two ages straight: sixteen to drive, twenty-one to supervise. Next, we prepare for the drive test itself.

why_how.text: The examiner checks the vehicle first because the test only goes ahead in a safe, insured and registered car.
Only you and the examiner ride along, so nothing interferes with how your driving is scored.

scenario.text: Ana books a drive test at a certified driving school and brings her family's car.

reasoning.text: The examiner checks the lights, signals, belts, windshield, tires, doors and windows, and the car's insurance and registration.

result.text: The car passes, Ana drives alone with the examiner, and if she fails she can retake the drive test the next business day.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing the next-business-day wait applies to the written knowledge test too.

correction.text: The next-business-day wait applies to a failed drive test, not to the written knowledge test.

memory_support.text: Safe car, two people, next day retake.

prompt.text: Ana fails her drive test on a Tuesday. When is the earliest she can retake it?

rationale.text: A failed drive test can be retaken on the next business day; that wait is about the drive test only.

narration.text: This lesson walks you through the drive test before the car even moves. Many people focus only on the driving, but the handbook spends real time on the setup: who gives drive tests today, what the examiner checks on your vehicle, who may be in the car, what happens if you fail, and how the examiner behaves. We finish with what the test actually measures, from the three skill categories to the six maneuvers that make up your score. Knowing all of this ahead of time removes surprises and lets you spend test day focused on careful, legal driving.

lines.text: State offices do not schedule them now.
Most are at certified driving schools.

narration.text: Start with where to go. State driver license offices do not currently schedule drive tests. Some county-run offices do, and most drive tests are given by certified commercial driving schools. That matters for planning: if you call a state office expecting to book a road test, you will likely be pointed elsewhere. When a practice question asks who gives most drive tests, the answer is the certified commercial driving schools, with some county offices also offering them. The state office is still where much of the licensing paperwork happens, but the road test usually is not.

lines.text: Doors and windows open from inside.

narration.text: Before the test starts, the examiner checks the vehicle for safety. That includes brake lights, turn signals, seat belts, the windshield and the tires, and the examiner confirms that the doors and windows open from the inside. If you supply the vehicle, it needs current insurance and registration. Once the car passes, the rules turn to the people inside. Only you and the examiner may be in the car: no interpreters, family, friends or pets. Remove any weapons, switch off the radio, phone and other electronics, and clear the dashboard and the rearview mirror so nothing distracts either of you.

lines.text: Failed drive test: next business day.
The wait is for the drive test.

narration.text: Here is a common trap. If you fail the drive test, you cannot retake it until the next business day. People sometimes carry that rule over to the written knowledge test, but the handbook ties the wait to the drive test. So when a question asks about retaking a failed road test, think next business day, not later the same afternoon and not weeks later. And if a question is really about the written test, do not import the drive test wait. Matching the rule to the right test is exactly what these questions are designed to measure.

lines.text: Never asked to break the law.

narration.text: The examiner will never ask you to break the law. If an instruction ever seems to require something illegal, that is not what is being asked. Ask any questions you have before the test starts, because you are scored the entire time, and extra talking only interferes with your focus. The test follows AAMVA guidelines and looks at three skill categories: perceptual skills, like seeing gaps and hazards; motor skills, like operating the controls; and attentional skills, like focusing and shifting your attention. Your score comes from six maneuvers, which the next lessons break down one by one.

lines.text: A failed drive test on Tuesday.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ana takes her drive test at a certified driving school on a Tuesday and does not pass. Her friend says she must wait thirty days, and her brother says she can try again that afternoon. Who is right? Neither of them. A failed drive test can be retaken on the next business day, so Wednesday is the earliest option if it is a business day. Remember that this wait belongs to the drive test, not the written knowledge test. Also remember that her car must pass the safety check again, and only Ana and the examiner may ride along.

lines.text: Book with a school or county office.

narration.text: Let us close the setup lesson. Most drive tests are given by certified commercial driving schools, with some county-run offices also testing, while state offices do not currently schedule them. The examiner checks your vehicle's lights, signals, belts, windshield, tires, doors and windows, and a car you supply needs current insurance and registration. Only you and the examiner ride along, with electronics off and the dashboard and mirror clear. Ask questions before you start, since you are scored the whole time. If you fail, you can retake the drive test on the next business day. Next come turns and signals.

why_how.text: Turn position matters because starting from the correct edge of your lane keeps your path predictable to others.
Signal distance gives other drivers time to react, which is why a faster four-lane highway needs a longer warning.

scenario.text: Sam prepares a right turn on a city street during the drive test.

reasoning.text: Sam signals for one hundred feet and moves to the right-most part of the lane before turning.

result.text: Sam finishes centered in the proper lane without touching the curb and cancels the signal within three seconds.

claim.text: Common mistake: starting a right turn from the center of the lane, or from the left side.

correction.text: A right turn starts from the right-most part of your lane, and a left turn from the left-most part.

memory_support.text: Right from right, left from left.

prompt.text: You are about to change lanes on a four-lane highway. How long must your signal stay on first?

answer.text: For two hundred feet before the lane change.

rationale.text: The urban distance is one hundred feet, but four-lane highways call for two hundred feet, and either way you cancel within three seconds.

narration.text: This lesson covers the parts of the drive test where most points are won or lost: choosing lanes, positioning for turns, and using your turn signal. Examiners grade lane selection and lane management closely, and they watch exactly where a turn begins and where it ends. Then come two numbers about signals: how far ahead you signal, which depends on the road, and how quickly you cancel afterward. None of these rules is complicated on its own, but they are easy to reverse under test pressure, so we will practice keeping each one in its proper place.

lines.text: Enter and leave from the correct lane.

narration.text: Lane selection is graded. You enter and leave traffic from the correct lane, approach intersections in the correct lane, and finish each maneuver in the correct lane. Lane management is graded too. You stay entirely within the turning lane, keep both hands on the wheel, and steer with an approved method such as hand-over-hand or push-pull-slide. The examiner is watching whether the car is where it belongs at every stage of a maneuver, not just whether you got around the corner. A one-handed, palm-on-the-wheel turn may feel smooth, but it is not an approved method.

lines.text: Right turn: right-most part of lane.
Left turn: left-most part of lane.

narration.text: Where a turn begins is precise. When turning right, start from the right-most part of your lane. When turning left, start from the left-most part of your lane. After the turn, settle the car in the center of the proper lane, and never cross lane markings or ride over curbs. Think of it as a clean entry and a clean exit. The entry hugs the side of your lane that matches the turn direction, and the exit puts you in the middle of the lane you were aiming for. Clipping a curb or drifting across a line costs points even if the turn felt fine.

lines.text: Or start from the lane center.
Match the side to the turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap the handbook calls out directly: candidates often reverse the starting positions or begin from the center of the lane. The fix is a simple matching rule. The side of the lane you start from is the same as the direction you are turning. A right turn starts from the right-most part of your lane, and a left turn starts from the left-most part. Starting from the center is not a safe middle ground; it is the mistake. When a practice question describes a driver drifting to the left before a right turn, you are looking at the error.

Signals follow two numbers. Keep your turn signal on continuously for one hundred feet before turning or changing lanes in urban areas, and for two hundred feet before doing so on four-lane highways. The higher speeds of a four-lane highway mean other drivers need more warning. After you finish the turn or lane change, cancel your signal within three seconds. A signal left blinking tells other drivers you are about to move again, which can be just as confusing as no signal at all. So the full habit is: signal early enough for the road, then cancel promptly once you are done.

lines.text: A lane change on a four-lane highway.
How far ahead do you signal?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a four-lane highway and want to change into the left lane. How far ahead must your turn signal stay on, and what do you do after the move? Answer before reading on. The signal stays on continuously for two hundred feet, because that is the distance for four-lane highways. One hundred feet is the urban distance and would be too short here. Once you are settled in the new lane, cancel the signal within three seconds. The cancel rule is the same on every road, while the distance depends on which kind of road you are driving.

lines.text: Correct lane in, correct lane out.
Right from right, left from left.
One hundred or two hundred feet, then cancel.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Lane selection means entering, approaching and finishing every maneuver in the correct lane, and lane management means staying inside the turning lane with both hands on the wheel and an approved steering method. Right turns begin from the right-most part of your lane, left turns from the left-most part, and every turn ends centered in the proper lane without crossing markings or riding over curbs. Signal for one hundred feet in urban areas and two hundred feet on four-lane highways, then cancel within three seconds. Next, we look at speed, stopping and searching.

why_how.text: Smooth speed and acceleration keep traffic flowing and keep you in control through turns and lane changes.
Physical searching is required because cameras and warnings can help but cannot see everything you can.

scenario.text: Jo pulls up behind a pickup at a red light during the drive test.

reasoning.text: Jo stops with no forward motion and leaves enough room to see where the pickup's rear tires touch the pavement.

result.text: When the light turns green, Jo accelerates smoothly without jerking or stalling.

claim.text: Common mistake: trusting a backup camera or blind-spot warning instead of looking over your shoulder.

correction.text: Driver aids may be used on the test, but they never replace your own physical searching.

memory_support.text: See the tires, scan left right left.

prompt.text: You stop behind a pickup at a red light. How do you know you have left enough space?

answer.text: You can see where the pickup's rear tires touch the pavement.

rationale.text: That view is the handbook's simple measure of a safe stopping gap behind another vehicle.

narration.text: This lesson covers the quieter skills the examiner scores on every block of the drive test. Speed control, stopping position, acceleration and searching rarely feel dramatic, but they show whether you are truly in control of the car. You will learn what good speed control looks like near intersections, what makes a stop correct, a simple way to judge your gap behind another car, what to avoid when you accelerate, and the scanning habits the handbook expects. We finish with a point that matters more every year: how driver-assist technology fits into the test, and where it falls short.

lines.text: Slow smoothly without holding up traffic.

narration.text: Good speed control means slowing smoothly without holding up traffic, keeping a steady speed through a lane change, and reaching an intersection slowly enough to turn without braking in the middle of the turn. A correct stop has no forward motion at all. It stays behind the stop line and the crosswalk, and the front wheels stay pointed straight until you actually begin the turn. Turning the wheels early while you wait is a small habit that costs points, and rolling over the line is treated as an incomplete stop. Each part of the stop is something the examiner can see clearly.

lines.text: No jerks, lugging, coasting or stalls.

narration.text: When you stop behind another vehicle, the handbook gives you an easy measure. You are far enough back if you can see where its rear tires touch the pavement. If the tires are hidden by your hood, you are too close. When it is time to move, accelerate smoothly. Do not jerk the car, lug the engine, coast, clash gears, stall, or hold up traffic. Smooth acceleration is about control and about the drivers around you, who expect you to move off at a steady, predictable pace. Both of these skills show up again and again during a normal city drive test.

lines.text: Cameras and warnings may be used.

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches drivers with newer cars. Backup cameras and blind-spot or lane-departure warnings may be used during the drive test. That part is allowed. But they never replace your own physical searching. You still check over your shoulder before a lane change, use your mirrors, and look around before moving. A practice question may describe a driver who changes lanes because the warning light stayed off; that driver skipped a required step. Treat every aid as a helper that adds information, never as permission to skip the looking the examiner is grading.

Here is a quick check: during your drive test you stop behind a pickup at a red light. How can you tell whether you left enough room, and what makes your stop itself correct? Decide before reading on. You are far enough back if you can see where the pickup's rear tires touch the pavement. Your stop is correct if the car has no forward motion, sits behind the stop line and crosswalk, and keeps its front wheels straight until you begin any turn. When the light changes, move off smoothly, without jerking, lugging the engine or stalling.

Let us review. Slow smoothly, hold a steady speed through lane changes, and reach intersections slowly enough to turn without braking mid-turn. Stop with no forward motion, behind the line and crosswalk, wheels straight. Leave enough room to see the rear tires of the vehicle ahead, and accelerate smoothly. Searching means scanning traffic, checking over your shoulder before a lane change, using mirrors, looking left, right, then left again before entering an intersection, and looking behind after every turn. Cameras and warnings can help, but they never replace that physical searching. Next, we turn to the rules for minor applicants.

why_how.text: Minors need an adult who accepts legal liability, which is why the affidavit comes before the permit.
The twelve-month permit hold and the fifty-hour log make sure a teen gains real supervised experience first.

scenario.text: Riley gets an instruction permit at fifteen and a half, with a parent signing the Affidavit of Liability.

reasoning.text: Riley is younger than sixteen and six months, so the six instructor hours apply along with the twelve-month hold and the log.

result.text: Riley completes six instructor hours and a fifty-hour log with ten night hours, then applies after twelve months.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the ten night hours are added on top of the fifty-hour log.

correction.text: The ten night hours are part of the fifty-hour total, not extra hours beyond it.

memory_support.text: Affidavit, a year on permit, fifty logged.

prompt.text: Riley's log shows fifty hours, and ten of them were at night. Is the log requirement met?

answer.text: Yes. Ten night hours inside fifty total hours meets the requirement.

rationale.text: The night hours are counted within the fifty-hour total rather than added to it.

narration.text: This lesson covers the extra steps for applicants under eighteen. Colorado adds them because new teen drivers benefit from time, supervision and an adult who takes responsibility. You will learn about the Affidavit of Liability and who may sign it, what signing means and what happens if the signer withdraws, how long a minor holds a permit, what goes into the driving log, and when behind-the-wheel training with an instructor is required. We finish with the substitute rule for families who live far from a qualifying driving school, which is narrower than many people assume.

Applicants under eighteen must include an Affidavit of Liability, form DR twenty-four sixty. It can be signed by a parent, stepparent, grandparent with power of attorney, legal guardian, spouse over eighteen, or another responsible adult who accepts legal liability. The affidavit is signed before a driver license office employee or a notary. Once signed, that person becomes legally responsible for your driving. Minors in foster care can be exempt under certain conditions. The point of the form is accountability: an adult is putting their own name behind the teen's driving, which is why the next rule about withdrawing has such weight.

lines.text: Withdrawal cancels the permit or license.
A spouse must be over eighteen.

narration.text: The adult who signs the affidavit is not locked in forever. The signer may withdraw, and withdrawing cancels the minor's permit or license. That gives the signer real influence over whether the teen keeps driving. The list of eligible signers includes a spouse, but only a spouse who is older than eighteen. So a seventeen-year-old's eighteen-year-old spouse does not qualify. When a practice question describes a signer who changes their mind, the result is cancellation of the permit or license, not a warning and not a fine. When it describes a young spouse, check the age line first.

lines.text: Ten of those hours at night.

narration.text: Time and practice come next. A minor must hold an instruction permit for twelve months before applying for a driver license. During that time the minor builds a signed driving log showing fifty hours of driving, including ten hours at night. Both requirements apply together: a full year on the permit and a completed log. The log is signed, which means a supervising adult vouches for those hours. A teen who has racked up fifty hours in three months still waits out the twelve-month hold, and a teen who has held a permit for a year still needs the full log.

Here is the trap. The minor log requires fifty total hours, of which ten must be at night. The night hours are part of the total, not added on top. So a log with forty daytime hours and ten nighttime hours meets the requirement, while a log with fifty daytime hours and no night driving does not. Questions sometimes offer sixty hours as a tempting answer, built by adding the ten to the fifty. Resist it. Fifty is the whole log, and ten of those fifty must happen after dark. Keep both numbers, and keep them nested inside each other.

lines.text: Under sixteen and six months: six hours.
Behind the wheel with an approved instructor.

narration.text: Some minors need one more piece. Applicants younger than sixteen and six months must also complete six hours of behind-the-wheel training with an approved driver education instructor. This is in addition to the twelve-month permit hold and the fifty-hour log. The age line is precise: sixteen and six months. An applicant who is older than that at application does not need the six instructor hours. This rule recognizes that the youngest new drivers benefit from professional instruction, not only from time with a parent. Pay attention to the age in any question about instructor hours before choosing an answer.

Here is a quick check: Riley has held a permit for twelve months and turns in a signed log showing fifty hours of driving, ten of them at night. Riley's friend insists the log is short because the night hours should be extra. Is Riley's log complete? Decide first. Yes, it is. The requirement is fifty total hours, and ten of those fifty must be at night; the night hours are counted inside the total. If Riley applied before turning sixteen and six months, Riley would also need six behind-the-wheel hours with an approved instructor, or the substitute where it applies.

lines.text: Twelve months, fifty hours, ten at night.
Substitute only without a nearby school.

narration.text: Let us pull it together. A minor needs an Affidavit of Liability signed before an office employee or notary by an eligible adult, and withdrawal cancels the permit or license. The minor holds a permit for twelve months and logs fifty hours, ten at night, inside the total. Applicants younger than sixteen and six months add six hours with an approved instructor. Only if no approved school within thirty miles of home offers at least twenty hours of behind-the-wheel training per week may twelve extra hours with a parent, guardian or alternate supervisor replace those six, with a printed route map when needed.

why_how.text: Passenger limits ease over time because a newly licensed teen gains experience before carrying young friends.
The first-year curfew keeps new minors off the road during the riskiest late-night hours.

scenario.text: Kai, seventeen, has been licensed for eight months and wants to drive two friends, ages seventeen and nineteen, to a game.

reasoning.text: Between six months and one year, a minor may carry only one passenger under twenty-one, apart from siblings and medical emergencies.

result.text: Kai takes one friend; after one year of licensure, Kai could carry as many passengers as there are seat belts.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a minor can carry one young passenger right from the first day of licensure.

correction.text: In the first six months, no passengers under twenty-one are allowed without a parent or another licensed adult driver.

memory_support.text: None, then one, then every belt.

prompt.text: Kai has been licensed for eight months. How many friends under twenty-one may ride along?

answer.text: One, unless the riders are siblings or it is a medical emergency.

rationale.text: Between six months and one year of licensure the limit is one passenger under twenty-one.

lines.text: Passengers step up over a year.

narration.text: Getting a license as a minor is not the end of the rules. For the first year, Colorado adds limits on who may ride with a teen driver and when that teen may be on the road. These limits change with time, so the key question in any practice scenario is how long the teen has been licensed. In this lesson you will learn the three passenger stages, the exceptions to the middle stage, the midnight-to-five curfew for first-year drivers, and the specific exceptions that allow certain late trips. Keep a timeline in mind as we go: first six months, then the rest of the year.

lines.text: Unless a parent or licensed adult driver rides along.

narration.text: For the first six months after a driver under eighteen is licensed, no passengers under twenty-one are allowed unless a parent or another licensed adult driver is in the car. This is the strictest stage. It does not matter whether the young passenger is a careful friend or wears a seat belt; without that adult driver present, the passenger cannot ride along. The rule targets the period when a new driver has the least experience and is most easily distracted. If a scenario says the teen was licensed two or three months ago, start here: no young passengers without an adult driver.

lines.text: After one year: one per seat belt.

narration.text: From six months to one year of licensure, a driver under eighteen may carry one passenger under twenty-one. Siblings are an exception, and so are passengers in a medical emergency. After one year, the number of passengers may equal the number of seat belts. So the rules loosen in two steps. First the teen can add one young passenger, with sensible exceptions for family and emergencies. Then, after a full year, the limit becomes the car's seat belts. Each step depends only on how long the teen has held a license, so always find that number in the question first.

lines.text: Six months to a year: one.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Questions often give you a teen, a few friends and a time since licensing, and the wrong answers mix up the stages. Under six months, the answer is no passengers under twenty-one without a parent or licensed adult driver. From six months to one year, the answer is one passenger under twenty-one, not counting siblings or a medical emergency. After one year, passengers may equal the number of seat belts. A teen licensed for two months cannot carry one friend, and a teen licensed for fourteen months is not limited to one. Count the months before anything else.

lines.text: Unless with instructor, parent or guardian.

narration.text: During the first year of licensure, a minor may not drive between midnight and five in the morning unless accompanied by an instructor, parent or legal guardian. There are exceptions. Trips to school or work are allowed with a signed statement, medical emergencies are allowed, and emancipated minors are excepted. The school or work exception is narrower than it sounds: the handbook ties it to a signed statement from the school or employer. Without that statement, a late shift alone does not excuse the trip. With it, the teen can make that trip home within the curfew window.

lines.text: Two young friends want a ride.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Kai is seventeen and has been licensed for eight months. Two friends, ages seventeen and nineteen, want a ride to a game, and neither is Kai's sibling. How many of them may ride with Kai, assuming no parent or adult driver comes along? Work it out first. Only one. Between six months and one year of licensure, a minor may carry one passenger under twenty-one, with siblings and medical emergencies as the exceptions. If Kai had been licensed for more than a year, both friends could ride, because the limit would then equal the number of seat belts.

lines.text: None, then one, then seat belts.
Signed statement for school or work.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. In the first six months after a minor is licensed, no passengers under twenty-one may ride without a parent or another licensed adult driver. From six months to one year, one passenger under twenty-one is allowed, with siblings and medical emergencies as exceptions. After one year, passengers may equal the number of seat belts. During the first year, a minor may not drive from midnight to five in the morning unless with an instructor, parent or legal guardian, except for school or work trips with a signed statement, medical emergencies, and emancipated minors.

why_how.text: A license can be suspended, revoked or canceled because the privilege depends on safe and honest conduct.
Crash conduct counts because stopping, sharing information, giving aid and reporting protect everyone involved.

scenario.text: After a minor crash in a parking lot, a driver leaves without stopping or exchanging information.

reasoning.text: Leaving a crash scene without stopping, exchanging information and giving aid is a listed ground for losing a license.

result.text: The driver can lose their license even though no points or impaired driving were involved.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing only points and impaired driving can cost you your license.

correction.text: Crash conduct, such as leaving the scene or not reporting under the Financial Responsibility Law, can also cost your license.

prompt.text: A driver with no points leaves a crash scene without exchanging information. Can that cost the license?

answer.text: Yes. Leaving a crash scene without stopping, exchanging information and giving aid is a ground for losing a license.

rationale.text: License loss is not limited to points or impaired driving; crash conduct counts too.

title.text: How a license can be lost

narration.text: This final lesson in the chapter looks at the other side of licensing: how you can lose the privilege. Colorado lists several kinds of conduct that can lead to a suspension, revocation or cancellation. Some are the ones everyone expects, like too many points or impaired driving. Others surprise people, like what you do or fail to do after a crash, or dishonesty on an application. Knowing the full list helps you answer practice questions, and it also explains why the duties you will learn in later chapters, such as stopping after a crash, carry such serious consequences.

lines.text: Refusing an alcohol or drug test.

narration.text: Your driving privilege can be suspended, revoked or canceled if you reach the point total for suspension, are convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or refuse an alcohol or drug test. Notice the third item. Refusing a test is its own ground, separate from being convicted. A driver cannot avoid consequences simply by declining to be tested. These three grounds share a theme: they track risky driving and impairment. Later chapters cover points and impaired driving in more detail, but for now, remember that refusal sits on the same list as the conviction itself.

lines.text: Not reporting under the Financial Responsibility Law.

narration.text: Crash conduct is its own category. Leaving a crash scene without stopping, exchanging information and giving aid, or failing to report a crash to the Division of Motor Vehicles under the Financial Responsibility Law, can cost you your license. Other grounds include lying on your application, not settling a crash judgment, lending or misusing your license, skipping a Division of Motor Vehicles re-examination, and a vehicular homicide conviction. The list shows that the privilege depends on honesty and responsibility as much as on driving skill. Handing your license to a friend is treated seriously, even if you never drive badly yourself.

lines.text: Leaving the scene is a ground.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners assume that only points or impaired driving can cost a license. The handbook says otherwise. Conduct after a crash, such as leaving the scene or not reporting it under the Financial Responsibility Law, can also cost you your license. So when a practice question describes a driver with a clean record who drives away from a collision without exchanging information, the right answer is that the license is at risk. Do not let the absence of points or alcohol in a scenario talk you out of it. Crash duties are licensing duties too.

title.text: A clean record, a bad exit

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver with no points and no history of impaired driving bumps another car in a parking lot and drives off without stopping or exchanging information. Can this cost the driver their license? Decide before reading on. Yes. Leaving a crash scene without stopping, exchanging information and giving aid is one of the listed grounds for losing a license. The same is true of failing to report a crash under the Financial Responsibility Law. License loss is not limited to points or impaired driving; crash conduct counts too.

Let us close the chapter. Your driving privilege can be suspended, revoked or canceled for reaching the point total, an impaired-driving conviction, or refusing an alcohol or drug test. Leaving a crash scene without stopping, exchanging information and giving aid, or failing to report a crash under the Financial Responsibility Law, can also cost you your license. Other grounds include lying on your application, not settling a crash judgment, lending or misusing your license, skipping a re-examination, and a vehicular homicide conviction. Keep the whole list in mind; the privilege depends on safe and honest conduct.
